What the official sources say

  • Step one: apply in writing to the selectmen or assessors for an abatement by March 1 following the date of notice of tax. (RSA 76:16, I(b); source)
  • If the notice of tax is on or before Dec. 31, the BTLA appeal deadline is September 1 (but no earlier than the municipal decision or July 1); if after Dec. 31, it is 8 months after the notice of tax. (Property Tax | Board of Tax and Land Appeals; source)
  • BTLA appeal filing fee is $65 by check or money order payable to Treasurer, State of NH. (Property Tax | Board of Tax and Land Appeals; source)
  • After 2 years from execution of an unredeemed real estate tax lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder. (RSA 80:76, I; source)
  • A municipality may refuse a tax deed; the lien then remains indefinitely and the right of redemption continues with interest. (RSA 80:76, II-a, III; source)

Who sets and collects property tax in New Hampshire?

Each city and town assesses, levies and collects its own property tax, and the state does not bill homeowners directly. The Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) states that local property taxes are assessed, levied and collected by municipalities under RSA 76 and the Rev 600 rules. DRA's Property Bureau monitors assessing practices, reviews municipal records and oversees revaluations.

That means the person you deal with when you sell is a local one: the assessor for value questions, and the tax collector for payoffs and liens. Two houses with the same price in neighboring towns can carry very different bills, because each municipality sets its own rate.

Under RSA 76:2, the property tax year runs from April 1 to March 31, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken in April of that year. If you sell in the fall, your April 1 assessment still drives the bill that arrives, and that matters when you are working out what you owe at closing.

When are New Hampshire property taxes due?

In towns and cities that bill twice a year, a partial payment is due July 1 and the balance is due December 1. That is the schedule in RSA 76:15-a.

  • The July 1 bill is a partial payment computed from the prior year's assessed value times one-half of the previous year's tax rate.
  • Assessors commit the lists to the collector by May 15, and bills for the partial payment go out no later than June 15.
  • The remainder of the taxes assessed April 1, minus the July payment, is due December 1.

Not every municipality uses that pattern. Concord's tax page describes four quarterly bills in July, October, January and March, based on the prior April 1 assessment. Check your own town's collector page, since the due dates on your bill control.

Interest at 8 percent per annum is charged on taxes not paid by December 1 after their assessment, under RSA 76:13. Hampton's town page describes the same 8 percent rate, calculated daily starting the day after a bill is due.

What happens if the taxes are not paid? Tax liens and tax deeds

An unpaid bill can become a real estate tax lien, and an unredeemed lien can end in a tax deed. The pieces below come from RSA 80, the collection chapter, in municipalities that have adopted the lien procedure.

  • The collector must send notice of the impending lien at least 30 days before executing it, by certified or registered mail, return receipt requested (RSA 80:60).
  • Only the municipality, the county or the state can hold a tax lien on land and buildings (RSA 80:63).
  • Anyone with a legal interest in the land can redeem by paying the lien amount plus interest at 14 percent per annum from the execution date, any time before the collector gives a deed (RSA 80:69).
  • After 2 years from execution of an unredeemed lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder (RSA 80:76).

The sharp step up from 8 to 14 percent is why owners behind on taxes tend to feel the pressure after a lien is executed. If you are in that position and thinking of selling, the redemption payment is usually part of what has to be paid out of the proceeds.

How do I appeal my New Hampshire property assessment?

Start with a written abatement application to your town's selectmen or assessors, due by March 1 following the date of the notice of tax. That is the first step under RSA 76:16, and the form is prescribed by the Board of Tax and Land Appeals (BTLA). You must have complied with the RSA 74 inventory requirement.

StepDeadlineSource
Apply for abatement with the municipalityMarch 1 after the notice of taxRSA 76:16, I(b)
Municipality decides in writingJuly 1 after the notice of tax date; no response counts as denialRSA 76:16, II
Appeal to BTLA, notice of tax on or before Dec. 31September 1, but no earlier than the municipal decision or July 1BTLA
Appeal to BTLA, notice of tax after Dec. 318 months after the notice of taxBTLA
BTLA filing fee$65, check or money order to Treasurer, State of NHBTLA

The DRA explains that an abatement is a request to refund taxes based on physical description errors, damage to buildings during the tax year, or differences in opinion of value. If the town denies it, the next step may be an appeal to BTLA or the Superior Court.

The statute also requires the application to list specific reasons and any comparable properties. Vague complaints about the amount rarely help, so bring numbers.

Which exemptions and credits can lower the bill?

New Hampshire offers several exemptions and veterans' credits, and the owner has to apply for them. The DRA's permanent application, Form PA-29, goes to the municipal assessing officials by April 15 before the tax rate is set, and the assessing officials respond by July 1. Failing to respond counts as a denial, and a denial can be appealed to BTLA or Superior Court by September 1 after the notice of tax.

  • Elderly exemption (RSA 72:39-a): the applicant must be 65 by April 1 and a New Hampshire resident for three consecutive years, and income and asset limits apply.
  • Blind exemption (RSA 72:37): $15,000 off the assessed value unless the town votes more.
  • Veterans' tax credit (RSA 72:28): $50 standard, with towns able to adopt $51 up to $750.
  • Service-connected total disability credit (RSA 72:35): $700 standard, with towns able to adopt up to $5,000.
  • Disabled exemption (RSA 72:37-b): only where the town has adopted it.

The qualification date is April 1 of the tax year, per the PA-29 form. If you sell and move before the next April 1, check how that affects the credit with your assessing office. Exemptions are tied to a person and a home, so the buyer will have to apply for their own.

What should a seller do about taxes at closing in New Hampshire?

The practical task is to confirm with the tax collector what is owed, including any lien amount, before closing day. Ask for a written payoff figure and whether a lien has been executed on the parcel.

  • Pull your most recent bill, plus the previous year's if any part is unpaid.
  • Ask the collector whether a notice of impending lien has been sent, and when interest started.
  • If a lien exists, ask for the redemption amount to the expected closing date, since interest at 14 percent per annum keeps running.
  • Budget for the transfer tax: $.75 per $100 of the price from the seller and the same from the buyer, paid by stamps from the register of deeds, according to the DRA.

If back taxes, a lien and repair needs all stack up, an as-is cash sale can be a cleaner way out because the buyer is not waiting on a lender's appraisal. We do not promise a price or a timeline here, and we suggest speaking with your collector and a New Hampshire attorney for your exact numbers.

More questions about New Hampshire Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in New Hampshire?

Your city or town does. Local property taxes are assessed, levied and collected by municipalities under RSA 76, and the state Department of Revenue Administration monitors assessing practices.

When are New Hampshire property taxes due?

In towns that bill twice a year, a partial payment is due July 1 and the balance December 1. Some municipalities bill quarterly, so follow the due dates printed on your own bill.

What interest rate applies to late property taxes in New Hampshire?

Eight percent per annum on taxes not paid by December 1 after assessment under RSA 76:13. Once a lien is executed, redemption carries interest at 14 percent per annum under RSA 80:69.

What is the deadline to ask for an abatement?

March 1 following the date of the notice of tax. The municipality must decide in writing by July 1, and failure to respond is a denial.

How much does it cost to appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals?

The BTLA filing fee is $65, paid by check or money order payable to Treasurer, State of NH.

Can I sell a New Hampshire house with a tax lien on it?

A person with a legal interest can redeem by paying the lien amount plus 14 percent per annum interest before the collector gives a deed. In a sale, that payoff is usually handled out of the proceeds at closing.

When can a town take a house for unpaid taxes?

After 2 years from execution of an unredeemed real estate tax lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder under RSA 80:76. A municipality may refuse a tax deed, in which case the lien remains and the right of redemption continues.

title: New Hampshire Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home
content:
New Hampshire Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • New Hampshire Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • NH homestead right protects $400,000 of a person's homestead (or interest in it) from creditors (asset-protection, not a property tax exemption). (RSA 480:1, I; source)
  • To claim it the residence must have been a primary residence continuously for the previous 12 months; sale proceeds are protected if reinvested within 6 months in a new primary residence. (RSA 480:1, II; source)
  • Property tax elderly exemption requires 3 consecutive years of NH residence before April 1, and income and asset limits set by the town or city, no lower than $13,400 single / $20,400 married income and $35,000 net assets. (RSA 72:39-a; source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is the New Hampshire homestead exemption?

The New Hampshire homestead right is a creditor protection under RSA chapter 480 that shields up to $400,000 of a person's homestead, or of their interest in it, and it is separate from the property tax exemptions that towns grant. Many people search for the "homestead exemption" expecting a tax break, as in other states. In New Hampshire the tax relief comes from different statutes and is set town by town.

This page covers both, because a homeowner who is selling will meet both. The homestead right matters when a creditor, a lien or sale proceeds are in play. The property tax exemptions matter when a bill is due or an application has to move with you to a new home.

How much does the homestead right protect?

RSA 480:1, as amended with an effective date of January 1, 2026, entitles every person to $400,000 worth of their homestead or their interest in it. Amounts have changed over time, so check the date on anything you read.

PointWhat RSA 480:1 says
Amount$400,000 per person
Property typesIncludes manufactured housing you own and occupy, mobile homes, housing cooperatives and condominiums, if occupied as a dwelling
Occupancy testPrimary residence continuously for the previous 12 months
Sale proceedsProtected if reinvested within 6 months in a new primary residence
Combined ceilingParagraph III sets a total of not more than $550,000, or $400,000 for a single person
Medical debtFull market value may be claimed for debts from terminal or catastrophic injury or illness
TrustsA beneficiary of a qualifying trust that owns the property may claim it

The statute is at RSA 480:1. It protects equity from creditors. It does not lower your tax bill.

When does the homestead right not protect the house?

RSA 480:4 says the homestead right does not erase any debt, and it lists the cases where the protection does not apply. Knowing the list helps a seller judge whether a lien will follow the sale.

  • The collection of taxes.
  • Liens to collect on forfeited bail bonds or domestic support obligations.
  • Liens of mechanics and others for debts created in constructing, repairing or improving the homestead.
  • Enforcement of mortgages made a charge on the property according to law.
  • Liens filed by homeowner associations or by condominium associations under RSA 356-B for unpaid assessments, including collection costs.
  • Debts that existed when the homestead was purchased, unless the reinvestment rule in RSA 480:1, II applies.
  • The levy of executions as provided in the chapter.

A homestead claim, in other words, will not hold off a mortgage lender or a tax collector. It is aimed at ordinary unsecured creditors.

What happens to the homestead right when I sell?

The sale proceeds stay protected only if they are reinvested in a new primary residence within 6 months (RSA 480:1, II). A seller who takes cash from a house sale and does not buy another primary residence inside that window should not assume the money still carries the homestead shield.

The 12-month rule works the other way when you buy. To claim the homestead right in a new house, the residence must have been your primary residence continuously for the previous 12 months, and the reinvestment clause is the exception that carries protection over from the old house to the new one.

If you are selling because of debt, speak with a New Hampshire attorney before closing. Our team buys houses as-is for cash and can work around a closing date you choose, but we cannot tell you how a creditor will treat your proceeds.

Which property tax exemptions can a New Hampshire homeowner get?

New Hampshire towns and cities grant property tax exemptions and credits under RSA chapter 72, and the dollar amounts vary by municipality. The Department of Revenue Administration notes that local property taxes are assessed, levied and collected by municipalities under RSA 76. Manchester's assessors list the following, as one example of what a city adopts:

  • Elderly exemption under RSA 72:39-a, with assessed value deducted of $240,000 for ages 65 to 74, $325,000 for ages 75 to 79 and $435,000 for age 80 and over.
  • Blind exemption of $240,000 assessed value.
  • Disabled exemption of $240,000 assessed value.
  • Veterans credit of $500 toward taxes due, with a $2,000 credit for disabled veterans and $2,000 for surviving spouses.
  • Tax deferral, with total deferrals limited to 85 percent of assessed value.

Another town may adopt different numbers. Always read your own town's assessing page rather than assuming Manchester's amounts.

Who qualifies for the elderly exemption?

The elderly exemption requires three consecutive years of New Hampshire residence before April 1 of the year the exemption is claimed, plus income and asset limits the town or city sets (RSA 72:39-a). The statute puts floors under those limits: not less than $13,400 net income for a single person or $20,400 for married persons, and not less than $35,000 in net assets, excluding the person's residence and its land up to the greater of 2 acres or the minimum single-family lot size.

RSA 72:39-b adds the age brackets. A town may grant a different dollar amount to a person aged 65 up to 75, 75 up to 80, and 80 or older, and the exemption cannot be less than $5,000 in any category. A person who has been married to an owner for at least 5 consecutive years can qualify through a spouse's ownership. When an owner dies, the combined net asset amount for married persons continues to apply to the surviving spouse until the property is sold or transferred, or until the surviving spouse remarries.

How and when do I apply for a property tax exemption?

You file a permanent application with your town's selectmen or assessors by April 15 before the tax rate is set, on the state form (RSA 72:33). The application is signed under penalty of perjury and shows that you own the property and were qualified on April 1 of the first year.

The deadline has a safety valve. If accident, mistake or misfortune prevented you from filing on time, the assessors may accept a late application, but not after the local tax rate has been approved for that year.

  • One filing normally carries forward each year as long as you do not change residence.
  • Assessors can ask for periodic re-qualification no more than once a year, and failing to respond can cost you the exemption for that year. Manchester says existing exemptions continue automatically but are subject to annual re-qualification or audit.

What if the town denies my exemption?

An appeal goes to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to superior court, and it must be filed no later than September 1 following the notice of tax (RSA 72:34-a). The BTLA form requires a nonrefundable $65 check payable to the Treasurer, State of New Hampshire.

If your town bills twice a year, the notice of tax date is the final bill that sets your tax liability, so you appeal after that bill and not before. The exemption appeal covers only the exemption. An appeal of the assessment itself is a separate filing under RSA 76:16.

What do I do with my exemption when I sell my house?

Tell the assessor, because an exemption attaches to your qualifying residence and does not travel with the sale. RSA 72:33, II requires a person who changes residence after filing a permanent application to file an amended permanent application by December 1 following the move. Manchester's assessors ask owners who hold an elderly exemption or veterans credit and are selling or moving to say so, so the exemption can be applied to the new home.

The tax year matters at closing. New Hampshire's property tax year runs April 1 to March 31, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken in April (RSA 76:2). Towns that bill semiannually send a partial payment bill due July 1 and the remainder due December 1 (RSA 76:15-a). Your closing agent will prorate the current bill, so ask the town for the amount and status before the sale.

Our team buys New Hampshire houses as-is, and we can discuss timing around a tax bill if you call.

More questions about New Hampshire Homestead Exemption

Does New Hampshire have a homestead exemption for property taxes?

Not under that name. The homestead right in RSA chapter 480 protects up to $400,000 of equity from creditors. Property tax relief comes from separate exemptions and credits under RSA 72, which each town or city adopts and sets.

How much is the New Hampshire homestead right worth?

It is $400,000 per person under RSA 480:1 as amended effective January 1, 2026, with a combined ceiling of $550,000 stated in paragraph III.

What is the deadline to apply for a New Hampshire property tax exemption?

April 15 before the tax rate is set (RSA 72:33). The assessors can accept a late application for accident, mistake or misfortune, but not after the local tax rate has been approved for that year.

Can I keep my elderly exemption if I move?

Not automatically. You must file an amended permanent application by December 1 after the change of residence under RSA 72:33, II, and the new town's own limits and amounts will apply.

Are sale proceeds protected by the homestead right?

Proceeds from a qualifying residence are protected if reinvested within 6 months in a new primary residence (RSA 480:1, II).

title: New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • NH Legacy & Succession Tax (RSA 86) was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003. (Inheritance & Estate Tax | NH DRA; source)
  • For deaths on or after January 1, 2005, the NH Estate Tax return is not required due to repeal of the federal estate death tax credit. (Inheritance & Estate Tax | NH DRA; source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does New Hampshire have an estate tax or inheritance tax?

No. New Hampshire repealed its inheritance tax (the Legacy and Succession Tax) for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and its separate state estate tax return is no longer required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

The Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) explains the second step this way: the state estate tax depended on a federal credit, and when the federal estate death tax credit was repealed, the NH Estate Tax return was no longer required. A third tax, the transfer tax on personal property of nonresident decedents (RSA 89), was repealed for the same 2003 deaths.

For an heir deciding whether to sell an inherited New Hampshire house, that means no state death tax bill sits between you and the sale. Other costs still apply, and they are covered below.

What did the old New Hampshire death taxes look like?

The old Legacy and Succession Tax was an inheritance tax that fell on certain heirs, not on the estate as a whole. It only matters now if you are dealing with a death before 2003, which is rare but possible in a long-unsettled estate.

TaxStatusApplies to deaths
Legacy and Succession Tax (RSA 86)RepealedOn or after January 1, 2003
Transfer tax on nonresident decedents' personal property (RSA 89)RepealedOn or after January 1, 2003
NH Estate Tax return (NH-706)Not requiredOn or after January 1, 2005

Under the old rules, the DRA says a tax return was due nine months from the date of death. Spouses, children, parents, grandparents and grandchildren were among the non-taxable legatees. Brothers, sisters, nieces, nephews, friends and other non-relatives were among the taxable ones. The old NH-706 filing threshold was $675,000 for deaths in 2000 and 2001 and $1,000,000 for 2002 through 2004.

Does the federal estate tax matter for a house sale?

Only for large estates. The IRS lists the basic exclusion amount for a 2026 death at $15,000,000, and that is also the filing threshold for an estate tax return for a 2026 death.

The IRS lists the annual gift tax exclusion for 2026 gifts at $19,000 per donee. An estate whose gross value falls below the exclusion generally has no federal estate tax to pay, so most New Hampshire families selling a parent's house are not affected.

  • Check the date of death, because the exclusion amount is set by year of death.
  • Add up the whole estate, not just the house.
  • If the estate is near the threshold, ask an estate attorney before you sell.

What taxes can an heir still owe when selling an inherited New Hampshire house?

The main ones are the state real estate transfer tax on the sale, property tax, and possibly federal income tax on gain. The transfer into your name is a different matter: the DRA says transfers by devise, intestate succession, or the death of a joint tenant are exempt from the real estate transfer tax.

The sale itself is taxed. The transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both buyer and seller, with a $20 minimum each for a price of $4,000 or less. Buyer and seller purchase stamps from the register of deeds in the property's county.

Within 30 days after the deed is recorded, the state expects the purchaser's and seller's declarations of consideration and an Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34).

  1. Transfer tax on the sale, for the seller's half
  2. Unpaid property tax and any recorded lien
  3. Federal capital gain tax, if the sale price is above your basis (see our capital gains guide)

The IRS directs people who inherit property to Publication 551 for their basis rules, so ask your preparer how it applies to this house.

How does probate affect selling an inherited house in New Hampshire?

The estate's executor or administrator is the person who normally sells, and the Circuit Court Probate Division supervises. The DRA tells people with questions about probating an estate to contact the Probate Court in the county where the decedent lived.

The court's booklet, Administering an Estate, says an executor is named in a will and an administrator is appointed when there is no named executor. It tells the person in charge to try to get the best price when real estate or personal property is sold. The Judicial Branch also provides a Motion and License to Sell Real Estate to Pay Demands, used when an executor or administrator wants a license to sell the property to pay debts or claims against the estate.

When the work is done, the executor files a final accounting on the Executor's/Administrator's Accounting form (NHJB-2117-Pe) so that the duties can be released.

Our New Hampshire probate guide covers the court steps in more detail.

Who pays the property tax on an inherited house while the estate is open?

The property keeps being taxed in the meantime, and the estate or the heir who holds it is responsible for the bill. New Hampshire's tax year runs April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2), so a house can generate two bills while probate is still pending.

Unpaid tax carries 8 percent interest under RSA 76:13. Once a lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 allows anyone with a legal interest in the land to redeem it by paying the lien amount with interest at 14 percent per year before the collector gives a deed.

  • File a change of mailing address with the town or city assessing office.
  • Ask the tax collector for a current payoff before listing.
  • Note that a new deed can take 30 days or more to reach the assessing office after a transfer, according to Manchester's tax collector.

Where can you get official answers about death taxes in New Hampshire?

Call the DRA Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 for state questions, or write to NH DRA, Estate & Legacy, PO Box 457, Concord, NH 03302-0457. The DRA's inheritance and estate tax pages are the place to confirm that no state return is needed for a recent death.

For federal questions, the IRS estate tax page lists the filing threshold by year of death, and its Form 706 instructions explain the return for estates that exceed it. For the court side, the Probate Division of the Circuit Court handles wills, trusts and estates, and the county where the decedent lived decides where the case is filed.

Keep every answer in writing. A title company will want to see that the estate has authority to sell and that taxes and liens are cleared before it closes.

What are your options if you inherited a New Hampshire house you do not want?

You can keep it, rent it, sell it on the open market, or sell it as-is to a cash buyer. The tax picture above stays the same for each, and the differences are in time and repair cost.

An as-is cash sale can suit an estate with a house that needs work, back taxes or out-of-state heirs, because the buyer pays for the property in its present condition and the title company settles taxes and liens at closing. We make no promise about price here, since every house and every town is different.

Before choosing, gather the death certificate, the will or court appointment papers, the latest tax bill, and any lien notices.

More questions about New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does New Hampshire have an inheritance tax?

No. The Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, according to the DRA.

Is there a New Hampshire estate tax return to file?

Not for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. The DRA says the NH Estate Tax return is not required because the federal estate death tax credit was repealed.

Do I pay transfer tax when a house passes to me by will?

No. The DRA lists transfers by devise, intestate succession and the death of a joint tenant as exempt. A later sale by you is taxed at $0.75 per $100, split between buyer and seller.

What is the federal estate tax threshold in 2026?

$15,000,000 for a 2026 death, according to the IRS. Estates below that amount generally do not owe federal estate tax.

Who handles questions about probate in New Hampshire?

The Probate Court in the county where the decedent lived, part of the Circuit Court Probate Division. The DRA directs probate questions there.

New Hampshire Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • For residential tenancies, 30 days' eviction notice suffices; 7 days if the reason is nonpayment, substantial damage, behavior affecting health/safety, or domestic violence cotenant termination. (RSA 540:3, II; source)
  • Notice must state the reason with specificity; nonpayment notices must advise of the right to cure under RSA 540:9. (RSA 540:3, III-IV; source)
  • Restricted property may be terminated only for listed reasons including nonpayment, substantial damage, material lease violation, other good cause, and lease expiration with 60 days' notice for leases of 12 months or longer. (RSA 540:2, II; source)
  • After the notice expires the landlord obtains a landlord-tenant writ; the return day is 7 days from service; if the tenant appears a hearing is set within 10 days. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Tenant may cure nonpayment by paying back rent plus $15, up to three times in 12 months; money judgments in these cases are limited to $1500. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Court may stay the writ of possession up to 90 days if the tenant pays rent weekly; notice of intent to appeal is due within 7 days of the notice of judgment. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • A refusal of a rent increase noticed 30 days ahead, and legitimate business or economic reasons, can constitute 'other good cause' for terminating a restricted tenancy. (RSA 540:2, IV-V; source)
  • For residential tenancies, 30 days' eviction notice is generally required. (RSA 540:3, II; source)
  • Lease expiration is a ground only for leases of 12 months or longer, with 60 days' written notice and possessory action filed within 6 months. (RSA 540:2, II(i); source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How long does the eviction process take in New Hampshire?

The New Hampshire Judicial Branch describes an eviction as a short chain of dated steps: a written notice, a court writ, a return day, a hearing within about 10 days of the tenant's appearance, and a writ of possession that issues no sooner than 8 days after a loss at hearing. Add the notice period of 7 or 30 days and a landlord is looking at several weeks from first notice to a sheriff at the door, longer if the tenant appeals or asks for extra time.

That arithmetic matters when you own a rented house you want to sell. A buyer who needs the house vacant will ask for a date, and in this process only a court sets it. The sections below walk the steps in order, using the Judicial Branch video guide, the statutes in RSA 540 and the 603 Legal Aid walk-through.

What are the steps, in order?

There are nine usual steps, and the first happens outside the courthouse. The table lists them with the timing each source gives.

StepWhat happensTiming
1. Eviction noticeLandlord serves a written notice stating the reason7 or 30 days under RSA 540:3
2. WritLandlord files a landlord and tenant writ after the notice expiresSheriff serves the tenant
3. Return dayWrit goes back to the court; tenant files an appearance to contest7 days from service
4. HearingCourt schedules the merits hearingWithin 10 days after an appearance
5. JudgmentCourt issues a written decisionNot always the same day
6. Writ of possessionIssues to the landlord; only a sheriff carries it outNo sooner than 8 days after the hearing, per 603 Legal Aid
7. Discretionary stayTenant may ask for more timeJudicial Branch says up to 90 days if rent is paid weekly
8. Notice of intent to appealFiled at the circuit courtWithin 7 days
9. Supreme Court appealAppeal perfected at the New Hampshire Supreme CourtWithin 30 days

What does the landlord do before filing in court?

Before filing, the landlord serves the eviction notice and, for nonpayment, a demand for rent listing the unpaid dates and the amount owed. The Judicial Branch also tells landlords to record the date and time the papers were delivered in a certificate of service.

A nonpayment tenant still has the right to cure. Under RSA 540:9, paying all rent owed through the payment date, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and the landlord's filing and service fees before the merits hearing ends the case, and the landlord must file a receipt with the court. The cure is limited to 3 times in 12 months.

The court system also offers free remote mediation through its Office of Mediation and Arbitration at 603-271-6418, and the Judicial Branch recommends it as an optional step.

What is the landlord and tenant writ, and what is the return day?

The writ is the summons that starts the court case, and the return day is the date by which the signed writ must be back at the court and by which the tenant must file an appearance. Under RSA 540:13, the writ is returnable 7 days after the sheriff serves it.

The landlord can only file the writ after the eviction notice has expired, and must attach the expired notice, any demand for rent and the filing fee. A sheriff must serve it. Anyone can serve the eviction notice, but not the writ.

The return day is a filing deadline for the tenant and is not a hearing date. A tenant who files an appearance by then gets a hearing. A tenant who does not may be found in default, after which the court mails a default notice and, if the tenant does not respond, can issue a writ of possession. RSA 540:13 requires that default notice to be mailed at least 3 days before the writ issues.

603 Legal Aid also reports a new law effective October 8, 2026, requiring a tenant to file an answer within 5 days of the return day. Check the current court forms before you rely on the older appearance-only description.

What happens at the hearing?

At the hearing the landlord has to prove the grounds for eviction by a preponderance of the evidence, meaning more likely than not, and has to show strict compliance with the notice and, for nonpayment, the demand for rent. The Judicial Branch says that when a landlord seeks only possession, the court can consider only the defenses set out in RSA 540, such as retaliation or violation of the health and safety standard.

The landlord can also ask for unpaid rent in the same case. The tenant's offsets and counterclaims are then considered, and any money judgment is capped at $1,500 per decision, though either side may sue separately for more (RSA 540:13). The hearing notice must be mailed at least 6 days before the hearing.

The judge may rule from the bench or by mail. If the tenant wins, the tenant stays and the court can award costs. If the landlord wins, a judgment for costs and a writ of possession follow after a short period.

When can the tenant actually be made to leave?

A tenant has to leave only when a sheriff serves the writ of possession and orders them out, which is never on the day of a lost hearing. 603 Legal Aid says the writ is not given to the landlord any sooner than 8 days after the hearing, and that the landlord cannot serve it personally.

Two things can stretch the timeline:

  • A discretionary stay: the Judicial Branch says the court may delay the writ for up to 90 days if the tenant keeps paying rent weekly. 603 Legal Aid's tenant guide describes a shorter maximum, so ask the clerk which figure the court is applying to your case.
  • An appeal: a notice of intent to appeal must be filed within 7 days of the notice of judgment, and the appeal perfected with the Supreme Court within 30 days. In nonpayment cases the tenant pays a weekly amount set by the court during the appeal, and missing payments can bring a default on appeal and the writ of possession.

There is also a pay-and-stay route. A tenant may remain under an agreed schedule of timely payments, and missed payments can lead to eviction without another hearing.

What if the tenant is in the house because the landlord lost it to foreclosure?

Even then a judge's permission is required. 603 Legal Aid lists a tenant renting an apartment or single-family home that the landlord has just lost to foreclosure among those entitled to the full process, so a bank that takes the property has to go through the same steps.

In practice the tenant process above applies whoever ends up as landlord. Our separate New Hampshire foreclosure guide covers the lender side.

What mistakes slow a New Hampshire eviction down?

Most delays trace to notice errors or to self-help. The statute and the court materials point to a handful of repeat problems:

  • A notice that does not state the reason with specificity, or a nonpayment notice that leaves out the right to cure.
  • Filing the writ before the notice period has fully run.
  • No demand for rent in a nonpayment case.
  • Changing locks, cutting utilities or removing belongings before the sheriff acts. RSA 540-A:3 bars willful lockouts and utility shutoffs without judicial process, and a tenant can file a 540-A petition.
  • Throwing away belongings too fast. The landlord must take reasonable care of a former tenant's property for 7 days after the tenant leaves.

Each of these restarts the clock or exposes the owner to a claim. If you would rather not run the process at all, we buy New Hampshire houses as-is with tenants in place, and a conversation does not commit you to anything.

More questions about New Hampshire Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does an eviction take in New Hampshire?

It varies, but the steps have set limits: a 7 or 30 day notice, a return day 7 days after the writ is served, a hearing within 10 days of the tenant's appearance, and a writ of possession no sooner than 8 days after the hearing. A stay or appeal can add time.

Can a New Hampshire landlord evict without going to court?

No for a typical residential rental. The landlord must get a judge's permission, and only a sheriff can carry out the writ of possession. RSA 540-A:3 bars willful lockouts and utility shutoffs without judicial process.

What is the most a landlord can recover in an eviction case?

The money judgment in a landlord and tenant writ case is capped at $1,500 per decision. Either party can bring a separate suit for more (RSA 540:13).

Can the tenant appeal an eviction?

Yes. The tenant files a notice of intent to appeal within 7 days of the notice of judgment and perfects the appeal with the Supreme Court within 30 days, and keeps paying rent during the appeal.

Is mediation available for New Hampshire evictions?

Yes. The Judicial Branch offers free remote mediation through its Office of Mediation and Arbitration, reachable at 603-271-6418.

content:
New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Waiver of Administration under RSA 553:32 is a simplified probate process for testate or intestate estates; no inventory, fiduciary bond or accounting is required. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • The Waiver of Full Administration Statement (NHJB-2144-Pe) is filed no sooner than 6 months nor more than one year after the administrator's appointment, with no outstanding debts or claims. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Waiver of Administration also applies where the sole heir or beneficiary is appointed administrator, or all heirs/beneficiaries serve or assent. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where does probate happen in New Hampshire?

New Hampshire probate runs through the Probate Division of the Circuit Court, with probate judges sitting in courthouses in each of the state's ten counties. The Probate Division handles wills, trusts and estates, guardianships, adoptions, name changes, and equity matters such as partition and quiet title.

Estates that began electronically are e-filed at every probate location. The court's single toll-free number for the Circuit Court is 1-855-212-1234. Contested matters can be sent to a free probate mediation program, which matters if heirs disagree about whether to keep or sell the house.

The court supervises the estate, while the deed for any sale is recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies.

What are the main steps of a New Hampshire estate?

The court appoints an executor or administrator, who then inventories assets, pays debts, and distributes what is left. The Judicial Branch's estates self-help page points to its "Administering an Estate" booklet as the guide for fiduciaries.

  • A will, if there is one, and an application for appointment are filed with the Probate Division.
  • The fiduciary files an Inventory within 90 days after appointment, under RSA 554:1.
  • Debts, funeral costs and administration expenses are paid in the order RSA 554:19 sets.
  • The estate is closed by an accounting, a summary administration, or, for qualifying estates, a waiver of administration.

The Judicial Branch also notes a publication fee for estates that require one. It was raised to $55 on December 28, 2021, so check the current fee when you file.

What goes on the inventory when the estate owns a house?

Real estate is listed with its address, county, book and page from the Registry of Deeds, and an estimated value. The court's inventory overview says town tax records may be used as the estimate, an appraiser is not required unless the court orders one, and the amounts need not be exact.

Values are as of the date of death, and jointly held property is not listed. If the estimate turns out to be significantly off, the fiduciary can file an amended inventory or correct it in the accounting. The total also matters because it can affect the bond the court has already set.

If you plan to sell, a realistic value on the inventory helps later. A sale price far from the inventory figure invites questions from heirs and the court.

Can an executor sell the house, and does the court have to approve?

An administrator needs a court license to sell real estate when the personal estate is not enough to pay debts and legacies. RSA 554:17 requires the administrator to apply for the license, and neglecting to do so is treated as maladministration and a breach of the bond.

The court's Motion and License to Sell Real Estate to Pay Debts form shows how it works in practice. The fiduciary lists the property by county, book and page, totals the debts and assets, and states the shortfall.

  • The motion asks to sell at public auction or private sale.
  • A surviving spouse can assent to the sale, including the homestead right. If there is no spouse but minor children, a guardian of the minors consents.
  • The order's license is valid for two years from the date of the order.
  • A return of sale goes to the court within one year of the sale, and net proceeds are reported within 30 days of receipt.

RSA 554:33 adds that no such license issues later than two years after the executor or administrator was appointed. If the estate has plenty of cash and the will gives the executor power to sell, the path can differ, so ask the court or an attorney which route fits.

What is waiver of administration, and how does it help a seller?

Waiver of administration is a simplified process under RSA 553:32 that skips the inventory, the fiduciary bond and the accounting. The Judicial Branch explains it on its page, "What is Waiver of Administration?", and Justia's copy of RSA 553:32 lists who qualifies.

  • A will names one beneficiary who is appointed administrator, or all beneficiaries serve together, or a trust is the sole beneficiary.
  • There is no will and one heir, including a surviving spouse, is appointed, or all heirs serve together or consent to an appropriate person.
  • The court finds waiver appropriate.

The administrator closes the estate by filing an affidavit of administration between 6 months and 1 year after appointment. The statute sets no value cap and does not exclude real estate, but the affidavit has to list all real estate the decedent owned at death, with its location, book and page. It also has to state that, to the administrator's knowledge, there are no outstanding debts.

Waiver does not erase the duty to pay expenses and debts from estate assets. Any interested person may petition for full administration before the affidavit is filed.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a New Hampshire estate?

The statute keeps creditors on a short clock once an administrator is appointed. Under RSA 556:1, no action can be sustained against an administrator within six months after the original grant of administration, and not unless the demand has been shown to the administrator. Under RSA 556:5, suit must begin within one year after the original grant, with exceptions where the administrator has retained estate in hand.

ItemRuleSource
InventoryWithin 90 days after appointmentRSA 554:1, court inventory overview
Waiver affidavit6 months to 1 year after appointmentRSA 553:32
License to sell real estateNot issued later than 2 years after appointmentRSA 554:33
License validity2 years from the orderCourt form NHJB-2136-Pe
Suit against administratorWithin 1 year of original grantRSA 556:5
Creditor action on real estate if no administrationBarred after 2 years from deathRSA 556:29

RSA 556:29 says that if no administration was granted within two years of the date of death, no creditor can afterward maintain an action to reach the real estate. The details are fact-specific, so ask an attorney before relying on it.

Is there a New Hampshire inheritance or estate tax on the house?

No. The Department of Revenue Administration says the Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and that the New Hampshire estate tax return is not required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. Details are on the DRA inheritance and estate tax page.

The real estate transfer tax also has an exemption for inherited property. The DRA's transfer tax FAQ lists transfers by devise, by intestate succession and descent, and by the death of a joint tenant as exceptions. A later sale to a buyer is a different matter. That sale is taxable at $.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both buyer and seller, and the DRA says each side buys stamps from the register of deeds in the county where the property is located.

How does a fiduciary deed work when the estate sells?

The executor or administrator signs a fiduciary deed, which RSA 477:30 sets out in a statutory form. By signing, the fiduciary covenants that he or she was duly authorized to make the sale and followed the statute in doing so. The deed must be acknowledged, and it has to show the grantee's mailing address, under RSA 477:3.

A cash buyer can often work around a slow estate because the sale is as-is and does not depend on a lender's appraisal. Even so, the court steps above still apply. We buy houses in New Hampshire from estates and can coordinate with your attorney on timing, and we do not give legal advice.

More questions about New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Which court handles probate in New Hampshire?

The Probate Division of the Circuit Court, with probate judges serving courthouses in each of the ten counties. It handles wills, trusts, estates, guardianships and related equity matters.

How soon after appointment must the inventory be filed?

Within 90 days after appointment, under RSA 554:1. The inventory lists real estate with its county, book and page and an estimated fair market value, and town tax records may be used as the estimate.

Does an executor need court permission to sell inherited real estate?

If the personal estate is not enough to pay debts and legacies, an administrator must apply for a license to sell under RSA 554:17. The court's license is valid for two years, and no license issues later than two years after appointment.

Is there a way to skip the inventory and accounting?

Yes, in qualifying cases. Waiver of administration under RSA 553:32 skips the inventory, bond and accounting, and the estate closes with an affidavit filed between 6 months and 1 year after appointment.

Does New Hampshire have an inheritance tax?

No. The Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and no estate tax return is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

Is the transfer tax owed when heirs receive the house?

No. Transfers by devise, intestate succession or the death of a joint tenant are exceptions to the real estate transfer tax. A later sale to a buyer is taxable at $.75 per $100, paid by each side.

Can heirs mediate a dispute over the house?

Yes. The Probate Division has a mediation program in which probate-trained mediators can be assigned at no charge to the parties in contested matters.

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • NH does not have an income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages. (Interest & Dividends Tax | NH DRA; source)
  • The Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. (Interest & Dividends Tax | NH DRA; source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does New Hampshire tax the gain when you sell a house?

The New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) pages we opened list no state tax on the gain from selling a house. The state does not have an income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages, and its Interest and Dividends Tax has been repealed.

That leaves two other layers to plan for. The federal government taxes gain on a home sale unless an exclusion covers it, and New Hampshire charges a real estate transfer tax on the sale itself. If you want to be certain about your own return, call the DRA Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 or ask a tax professional, because this guide is general information.

  • State: no income tax on wages, Interest and Dividends Tax repealed
  • State: real estate transfer tax on the sale, paid by both sides
  • Federal: capital gain tax on any gain above the home sale exclusion
  • Local: property tax prorated or paid at closing

What was the Interest and Dividends Tax, and is it gone?

The Interest and Dividends (I&D) Tax was a tax on interest and dividend income, and it was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. It was never a tax on the sale price of a home.

People often mix it up with a capital gains tax because it was New Hampshire's only tax that reached investment income. The DRA's own page summarizes the rate history:

Taxable periodI&D Tax rate
Ending before December 31, 20235 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20234 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20243 percent
Beginning after December 31, 2024Repealed

The DRA points to Technical Information Release 2025-001 for the repeal and says the law is found in RSA 77 and Rev 900. If you are filing a final I&D return for an earlier period, the state's Granite Tax Connect portal is where those returns are filed.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work for a New Hampshire seller?

If you sell your main home, the IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. You have to pass both an ownership test and a use test.

You meet the ownership test if you owned the home for at least 24 months out of the five years before the sale. You meet the use test if you lived in it as a residence for at least 24 months of those five years. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months. On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.

  • You generally cannot claim it if you excluded gain on another home during the two years before this sale.
  • If you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even if all the gain is excludable.
  • Report on Form 8949 and Schedule D when required.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence-community members on qualified extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.
  • Publication 523 has the full rules, worksheets and exceptions.

An installment sale does not remove the exclusion. The IRS says it remains available even if you spread the gain over later years.

What federal capital gains rates apply above the exclusion?

A gain on a home held more than one year is long-term and is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent for most sellers, depending on taxable income. A gain on a home held a year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.

The IRS lists thresholds for taxable years beginning in 2025. We did not open a page with 2026 thresholds, so treat these as the most recent we could confirm.

RateSingleMarried filing jointly
0 percentUp to $48,350Up to $96,700
15 percent$48,350 to $533,400$96,700 to $600,050
20 percentAbove $533,400Above $600,050

The IRS notes a few exceptions. The part of a gain tied to unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent, which can matter if you rented the house and took depreciation. People with significant investment income may also owe the net investment income tax, and a large gain can require estimated tax payments.

If you sell at a loss on a personal home, the IRS says the loss is not tax deductible.

How is the gain calculated when the house was inherited or improved?

Gain is the amount you realize from the sale minus your adjusted basis. Basis is generally your cost, plus improvements that add value, minus items such as allowable depreciation.

The IRS says that if you received the property by gift or inheritance, your basis is figured under different rules, and it points to Publication 551, Basis of Assets, for them. We did not open that publication, so we do not state a step-up amount here. Get a date-of-death value from an appraisal and keep it with the estate papers, because that record is what a tax preparer will ask for.

  • Improvements: new roof, additions, major systems. Keep receipts.
  • Selling costs: ask your preparer which closing costs reduce the amount realized.
  • Holding period: the IRS notes that property acquired from a decedent has special holding-period rules, covered in Publication 544.

What New Hampshire tax do sellers actually pay at closing?

The real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, and both the buyer and the seller pay it. For a sale of $4,000 or less, each side pays a $20 minimum.

The DRA says the tax is governed by RSA 78-B and Rev 800. Buyer and seller buy stamps from the register of deeds in the property's county, and the register attaches them to the deed when it is recorded.

Within 30 days after the deed is recorded, both parties file their Declaration of Consideration (CD-57-P for the purchaser and CD-57-S for the seller) and the Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34) with the state. Filing and payment can be done through Granite Tax Connect.

  • Taxable: sales, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds, leases of 99 years or more
  • Exempt: gifts, transfers between spouses under a final divorce decree, corrective deeds, transfers to the state, a county or a municipality, and transfers by devise, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death

How does property tax fit into a New Hampshire sale?

New Hampshire's property tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under RSA 76:2, and taxes are assessed on the April inventory. Whoever owns the house on April 1 appears on the assessment, and the closing agent settles the split between buyer and seller.

Late taxes carry 8 percent interest under RSA 76:13. If a municipal tax lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 sets 14 percent interest per year on the recorded lien and lets anyone with a legal interest in the land redeem it before the collector gives a deed. The sale proceeds usually clear it through the title company.

For city specifics, our Manchester and Nashua guides cover those offices and dates.

What should you do before selling a New Hampshire house with a large gain?

Work out your basis and your exclusion before you sign, because those two numbers decide whether any federal tax is due. A seller who lived in the house for two of the last five years and has a gain under $250,000 may owe nothing federally, though the IRS still requires reporting in some cases.

  1. Gather the purchase closing statement and improvement receipts.
  2. Count your months of ownership and residence in the last five years.
  3. Check whether a 1099-S will be issued.
  4. Ask a preparer about estimated tax if a taxable gain is likely.
  5. Budget for the 0.75 percent transfer tax on your side.

A cash sale does not change these rules. It changes the timeline, so you can plan when proceeds arrive against any estimated tax payment your preparer expects.

More questions about New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does New Hampshire have a capital gains tax?

The DRA pages we reviewed show no state tax on gain from a home sale. New Hampshire has no income tax on W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for periods beginning after December 31, 2024. Federal tax can still apply.

How much gain can I exclude on a house sale?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home for at least 24 months of the last five years. The IRS also bars the exclusion if you used it on another home in the prior two years.

Who pays the New Hampshire real estate transfer tax?

Both buyer and seller pay it, at $0.75 per $100 of the price. Transfers by will, intestate succession and a joint tenant's death are exempt.

Do I report a home sale if I owe no tax?

Yes, if you receive Form 1099-S, the IRS says you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable. You also report it if you cannot exclude all the gain.

Is a loss on a personal home deductible?

No. The IRS states that losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home, are not tax deductible.

What the official sources say

  • Recording fee is $10 for the first page plus $4 for each additional page; mortgage discharges $15 first page. (RSA 478:17-g, I; source)
  • An additional $25 LCHIP surcharge applies to recording each deed, mortgage, mortgage discharge or plan; the grantee pays it on a deed. (RSA 478:17-g, II(a); source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where do you record a deed in New Hampshire?

You record it with the registry of deeds in the county where the land lies. RSA 477:3-a requires every deed or other conveyance of real estate to be recorded at length in that county's registry, and it says the document is not effective against bona fide purchasers for value until it is recorded.

New Hampshire has ten county registries: Belknap, Carroll, Cheshire, Coos, Grafton, Hillsborough, Merrimack, Rockingham, Strafford and Sullivan. The NHDeeds.org directory links to each county site, and every sale is recorded at the registry for its own county. A parcel that crosses a county line is recorded in each county it touches.

Recording also drives validity against outsiders. Under RSA 477:7, a deed of bargain and sale, mortgage or other conveyance is not valid to hold the property against anyone but the grantor and the grantor's heirs unless it is acknowledged and recorded. For a seller, that is why the closing is not finished until the register has the deed.

What does a deed need before the register of deeds will accept it?

The deed must be signed by the grantor and acknowledged before a justice, notary public or commissioner, and it must show the grantee's mailing address. That is the rule in RSA 477:3. RSA 478:4-a adds recording requirements the register enforces.

  • The latest mailing address of each grantee.
  • The names of all municipalities where the property lies, in the first sentence of the first description paragraph.
  • The name of each person signing, printed or typed under the signature.
  • A document that is suitable for reproduction under the standards the registers of deeds adopt and post.

The statute also says documents should be on material, with markings and in a size, that ensure suitable permanent recording (RSA 478:4). Because the standards come from the registers, call or check the county website for the current layout rules before you send paper.

Which type of deed is used for a sale?

New Hampshire has statutory short forms, and a deed in substance following one carries the covenants the statute attaches to it. RSA 477:27 covers the warranty deed, RSA 477:28 the quitclaim deed, RSA 477:30 the fiduciary deed, and RSA 477:31 the foreclosure deed under power of sale.

The fiduciary form is the one an executor or administrator signs for an estate. By its terms, the grantor covenants that he or she was duly authorized to make the sale and complied with the statute. Sellers of inherited houses should read our probate page for the court steps that come first.

Choosing between warranty and quitclaim language is a legal decision, and it changes what the seller promises about title. A New Hampshire attorney or the closing attorney can tell you which fits your sale.

How much does it cost to record a deed in New Hampshire?

The recording charge is $10 for the first page and $4 for each additional page, plus a $25 surcharge for the Land and Community Heritage Investment Program (LCHIP). The fees are set by RSA 478:17-g. On a deed, the grantee pays the $25 surcharge.

By that math, a two-page deed costs $14 to record, plus the $25 surcharge. The surcharge is not assessed when the United States, the state, a county, a municipality, a village district or a school district is a party. Copies and other services are charged at rates each register posts.

How does the real estate transfer tax work at recording?

New Hampshire taxes the transfer itself, at $.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, and both the buyer and the seller pay. The Department of Revenue Administration's transfer tax FAQ says each side buys stamps from the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, the register affixes them to the deed, and the deed is recorded.

  • For illustration, a $400,000 sale means $3,000 from the seller and $3,000 from the buyer at that rate.
  • When the consideration is $4,000 or less, the minimum is $20 from each side.
  • Related-party transfers with unsupported stated prices are assessed on fair market value.
  • Foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds and easements are taxable transfers.
  • Exceptions include transfers by devise or intestate succession, transfers on the death of a joint tenant, and transfers between spouses under a final divorce decree.

Within 30 days after recording, each side must file a Declaration of Consideration (Form CD-57-P for the buyer, CD-57-S for the seller) and an Inventory of Property Transfer (Form PA-34) with the department. The DRA points filers to its Granite Tax Connect portal.

Can you record a New Hampshire deed electronically?

Yes, in principle. New Hampshire adopted the Uniform Real Property Electronic Recording Act, effective February 6, 2022 (RSA 478-A), and RSA 478-A:3 addresses the validity of electronic documents and recording of tangible copies of them.

What each county accepts and how it processes e-recording varies by registry, so confirm with the register before you plan around a same-day record. Most sellers never file the deed themselves, since the closing attorney or title company handles it.

If you are selling for cash, ask early who will record, what the cost is, and when the stamps will be bought. The register will refuse a deed that lacks the grantee's mailing address, the municipality names or the printed signer names, so those details are worth checking before closing day.

What about manufactured homes and trusts?

The transfer tax treats these differently, and the DRA FAQ spells out how. For manufactured housing, tax on most transfers is paid to the register of deeds in the county where the unit is located, by both buyer and seller. If the unit moves into New Hampshire from another state, only the buyer pays, and if it moves out of the state, only the seller pays.

A transfer into a revocable trust is taxable unless an exception applies, though the measure of the tax can be the minimum tax when the trust is created for estate planning as a testamentary substitute and the transfer is between the trust and its grantor. Transfers to or from an irrevocable trust are not taxable if the elements of a gift are met or an exception applies.

More questions about New Hampshire Recording a Deed

Where do I record a deed in New Hampshire?

With the registry of deeds in the county where the land lies. RSA 477:3-a says the deed is not effective against bona fide purchasers for value until it is recorded there.

How much does it cost to record a deed in New Hampshire?

$10 for the first page and $4 for each additional page, plus a $25 LCHIP surcharge on each deed, which the grantee pays. Transfer tax is separate.

What is the New Hampshire transfer tax rate?

$.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, imposed on both the buyer and the seller. Each side buys stamps from the register of deeds.

What forms are filed after recording a deed?

A Declaration of Consideration from each side (CD-57-P and CD-57-S) and an Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34), within 30 days after recording.

What must a New Hampshire deed show to be recorded?

The grantee's latest mailing address, the municipalities where the property lies in the first description sentence, and each signer's printed name. It must be acknowledged and suitable for reproduction.

Is inherited property subject to transfer tax?

Transfers by devise, intestate succession or the death of a joint tenant are exceptions to the tax. A later sale of the house is taxable.
